In the recording, al Qaeda’s second-ranking figure, Ayman al-Zawahiri, said Obama was the “direct opposite of honorable black Americans” such as Malcolm X. The imams described al-Zawahiri’s recorded remarks as “an insult” coming from people they said have “historically been disconnected from the African-American community generally and Muslim African-Americans in particular.”

“We find it insulting when anyone speaks for our community instead of giving us the dignity and the honor of speaking for ourselves,” the leaders said in a statement delivered at a news conference held at the Malcolm X and Dr. Betty Shabazz Memorial, Educational and Cultural Center.

The al Qaeda message, which ran 11 minutes and 23 seconds, was an Arabic-language audio recording with English subtitles. It was posted online Wednesday, though its authenticity has not been verified.

The speaker in the recording claimed Obama embodies the “direct opposite of honorable black Americans” like Malcolm X. He also said Obama, former Secretary of State Colin Powell, current Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, and “your likes” matched Malcolm X’s description of “house slaves.” The English version of the message used the phrase “house Negroes,” a term Malcolm X used for Black people he viewed as submissive to whites. The phrase refers to enslaved people who worked inside their white masters’ homes; Malcolm X contrasted them with enslaved people who worked in the fields, saying the former were more compliant.

Malcolm X, the prominent and fiery African-American Muslim activist of the 1950s and 1960s, was an early member and leader in the Nation of Islam. He broke with the organization in 1963 after becoming disillusioned with its leader at the time, Elijah Muhammed, but he continued to practice Islam. After receiving death threats for months, Malcolm X was killed in 1965 by Nation of Islam members, who shot him 16 times at close range. The three men convicted in his assassination have since been paroled.

Speaking Friday and invoking Malcolm X’s legacy, Imam Al-Hajj Talib ’Abdur-Rashid said Malcolm X “stood for human rights and the principle of self defense ... international law.” He added, “He would have rejected, and we who are Muslim African-Americans leaders reject, acts of political extremism.”

The Council on American-Islamic Relations also criticized Zawahiri’s remarks in a statement released Thursday.

“As Muslims and as Americans, we will never let terrorist groups or terror leaders falsely claim to represent us or our faith,” the group said. “We once again repudiate al Qaeda’s actions, rhetoric and world view and re-state our condemnation of all forms of terrorism and religious extremism.”

**Muslim African-American Leaders Reject al Qaeda Attack on Obama, Denounce Extremism**

*By Staff Writer*

Muslim African-American leaders strongly rejected an al Qaeda Internet message that attacked President-elect Barack Obama and attempted to invoke the language and legacy of Malcolm X, saying the message distorted Islam, misrepresented Black American Muslims and exposed the terror network’s political isolation.

The controversy erupted after al Qaeda’s deputy leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, released an online audio-video message criticizing Obama shortly after his 2008 election victory. In the recording, al-Zawahiri used a racially charged phrase associated with Malcolm X’s critique of Black leaders viewed as serving white power structures, applying it to Obama and other prominent Black American public figures, including former Secretary of State Colin Powell and then-Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice.

The message drew immediate condemnation from American Muslim organizations, particularly African-American Muslim leaders who said al Qaeda had no moral standing to speak for Islam, Black Americans or Muslims in the United States.

“Al Qaeda does not represent Islam, and it certainly does not represent African-American Muslims,” said one Muslim civil-rights leader in response to the recording. “Our community has struggled for justice, dignity and participation in American life. Extremists who murder innocent people have no right to claim our history or our heroes.”

Leaders said the attempt to cite Malcolm X was especially offensive. Malcolm X, who became a Sunni Muslim after leaving the Nation of Islam and making the pilgrimage to Mecca, remains one of the most important religious and political figures in African-American Muslim history. Community leaders said al-Zawahiri’s message ignored Malcolm X’s spiritual evolution and his later rejection of racial hatred.

“To use Malcolm X to justify terrorism is a betrayal of Malcolm X,” said an African-American imam. “He stood against oppression, but he also came to understand the universal brotherhood of Islam. Al Qaeda’s ideology is not liberation. It is violence, political manipulation and religious corruption.”

Muslim activists also defended Obama against the racial language used in the recording, even as many noted that Obama himself is a Christian and has repeatedly rejected false claims that he is Muslim. They said the controversy highlighted the burden placed on Muslim Americans during the 2008 campaign, when rumors about Obama’s background were often used to imply that being Muslim was itself suspect.

“We reject both sides of that smear,” said a Muslim African-American community organizer. “We reject al Qaeda’s attack on Barack Obama, and we reject the idea that calling someone a Muslim should be used as an insult. Muslim Americans are part of this country. African-American Muslims helped build this country.”

Several leaders said the message appeared designed to provoke division in the United States and to undermine goodwill generated internationally by Obama’s election. They argued that al Qaeda was threatened by Obama’s popularity in many Muslim-majority countries and by the symbolism of a Black American elected to the nation’s highest office.

“This is not strength; it is desperation,” said a Muslim civic leader. “Al Qaeda saw millions of Americans — Black, white, Latino, Asian, Muslim, Christian, Jewish and others — participate in a democratic election. That image weakens their claim that America is at war with Islam.”

The recording also criticized U.S. foreign policy and suggested that Obama would continue military actions in Muslim-majority regions. American Muslim leaders said criticism of government policy is legitimate, but they drew a sharp distinction between lawful dissent and extremist propaganda.

“We have always said that American foreign policy can and should be debated,” said an imam involved in interfaith work. “But there is no justification for terrorism. There is no Islamic justification for killing civilians. Those who preach that message are outside the moral teachings of our faith.”

African-American Muslim leaders emphasized that their community has a long history of civic engagement, military service, prison ministry, civil-rights activism and neighborhood institution-building. They said al Qaeda’s message erased that history in favor of a crude ideological appeal.

“Our mosques are feeding families, mentoring young people, fighting drugs and violence, and building bridges with churches and synagogues,” one leader said. “That is the reality of African-American Islam — not the hatred broadcast by men hiding in caves and sending messages over the Internet.”

The backlash reflected a broader effort by Muslim Americans to separate their faith from extremist movements that claim Islamic legitimacy. National Muslim organizations have repeatedly condemned al Qaeda, the Sept. 11 attacks and violence against civilians. African-American Muslim leaders said the latest message only reinforced the need to speak clearly.

“We will not allow extremists to define us,” said one community leader. “We will define ourselves — as Muslims, as African Americans and as Americans committed to justice and peace.”

The controversy also revived discussion of Malcolm X’s legacy and the way political movements compete to claim him. Scholars and religious leaders noted that Malcolm’s life cannot be reduced to a slogan. After his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, he spoke increasingly about human rights, global solidarity and the possibility of brotherhood across racial lines.

“Malcolm X challenged America to live up to its promises,” an imam said. “But he did not call Muslims to murder the innocent. Anyone who suggests otherwise is abusing his name.”

For many Muslim African-American leaders, the al Qaeda message was less an attack on Obama alone than an insult to a community whose history is deeply intertwined with both Islam and the Black freedom struggle.

“Black Muslims in America know something about racism, state power and injustice,” one leader said. “But we also know that faith requires moral discipline. Anger is not a program. Terrorism is not justice. And al Qaeda is not our voice.”
